#9964. AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere in healthcare, from doctors' intake forms to cancer screenings. But in some cases, life-and-death uses are outpacing cybersecurity.

Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point, now that AI is embedded throughout the patient life cycle and accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare," notes that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems, but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions and, more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, says Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open source AI tool for research and diagnosis because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for electronic health records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading.

Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury, like a left tibia fracture, could qualify as protected health information (PHI). That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, Biddle says.

AI's use is spreading fast, which complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection; like other industries, healthcare is also building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Some of AI's most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens, including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer at Check Point. It's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity, she adds.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks that administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to make sure that existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he says.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"We continue to see breaches of medical information, and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading.

To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data, rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produces an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she says.

The CISO question then becomes broader, she says, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?"

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," Sabaj says.

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, says he has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data — all considered PHI.

Englert cites recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings, which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, Englert warns. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing — any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and life cycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter says, and that should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint's Biddle has observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she says, noting that healthcare tends to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care.

"It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately," Biddle says.

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: "Why do you need to spend this amount?" says Biddle. It's difficult because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9963. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9962. GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

#9961. Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Researchers can't quite explain why cyber threats look so different in Italy compared with everywhere else.

To read this article in Italian, click here!

Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9960. [$] Portable Python scripts with dependencies

A basic Python script is portable: it can be copied between machines with little concern about compatibility. A script that depends on third-party packages requires quite a bit more care and consideration, however. In 2023, PEP 723 ("Inline script metadata") introduced a standard for declaring a Python script's dependencies inside the script itself. Several third-party tools can now automatically install and manage those dependencies, but there is still little official support for this standard within Python itself.

#9959. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9958. SourceHut disabled registration bypass | CVE-2026-121728

(plaintext version for nerds - patches welcome)

So, last time I wrote about account takeover using XSS on the CI platform of SourceHut.

This time I found something not nearly as ‘impactful’, but still interesting. Sorry for taking this long, but my SSD literally died1 and while waiting for a warranty repair I had to buy a used one (have you seen the prices yet??)2. It finally arrived so here I am.

So, if you want me to work faster, just drop me some money.3

Again, as you might know, I am not very excited about the current wave of natural language processing.4

No NLP has been used in this research. The mistakes are all mine.

SourceHut has been undergoing quite an architectural change. Its frontend was first built using Flask and Jinja templates and SQLAlchemy. But, for performance reasons, and for other reasons (decoupling of business logic, graphql) the API has been ported over to Go.

Back in 2021, while moving registration code from the frontend to the graphql backend, a subtle logic bug got introduced. While the frontend never shows a registration form, and states prominently ‘registration is currently closed’, the form handler is still there. It correctly states that registration is closed on every error path, but on the happy path it does not seem to ever check it. So if you happen to remember how to submit the form…

You just need to POST /register/step2 with your desired username, email and password. If the server in question disables registration, but has its SMTP configured properly (you still need to do email confirmation), boom, you are in.

There is no registration form displayed, so there is no token. However, fortunately for us attackers, the token from /login works just fine.

Does anyone know a bug bounty program where the researcher pays an upfront participation fee? I will set mine up this way for sure, and you should consider it too, if you are drowning in submissions.

#9957. Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

The enigmatic service is providing popular AI coding tools to mainland China and other regions where OpenAI and Anthropic products are not officially for sale — but with key security features turned off.

A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

#9956. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9954. Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

A four-question exercise that CISOs can use to create a threat model that promises results, without a big spend.

ISC2 Security Congress 2026 — Denver — A threat model should be a starting organizing principle for any security program. But rather than investing in a 200-page high-dollar threat model report, one longtime chief information security officer (CISO) argues that "four questions on a white board," can provide any team with an actionable plan forward.

Lora Vaughn, cybersecurity expert, former CISO, and now founder of her own consulting firm, The Vaughn Cyber Group, said that over her many years leading cybersecurity programs, she has developed a wickedly simple four-question threat modeling exercise that can be used in a wide range of organizations, be it the "National Security Agency (NSA) or your friendly neighborhood small-to-medium business (SMB)."

The answers, she said, can then offer a road map for investment decisions. That requires further exploration, she acknowledges, given there's always a new technology right around the corner that promises to drive down the cost of cybersecurity investment in enterprises. And reality must be balanced with industry hype.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

For instance, around 2015, the move to the cloud was supposed to put the onus on providers like AWS to protect enterprises. What came next was a flood of misconfigurations and misunderstandings about who owned which part of security. By 2018, the buzzword was "automation." But teams quickly learned that automating anything required defining buttoned-downed processes first — often a prohibitively time-consuming exercise that pushed many of these project timelines out. By 2021, zero-trust networks were on everyone's mind. But that turned out to be less of a prescription and more of a customizable, guiding principle; and, architecting a true zero-trust environment requires a big investment in systems that would prove to be a much longer journey than many in the sector had hoped.

And regarding the current zeitgeist, handing over enterprise security to an agentic AI model is a "fantasy," according to Vaughn, speaking from the stage while presenting her four-question threat model at ISC2 Strategic Congress in Denver this week.

"AI is a force multiplier," Vaughn said. "It just multiplies what you already have. Zero times anything is still zero. Math is undefeated."

Bottom line: Once the threat modeling is done, choose your path wisely, and with your eyes wide open. And recognize that it's an ongoing cycle. "Refresh the threat model quarterly," Vaughn added. "Or after any big change."

Ask yourself, if you walked into work at 8 a.m. Monday morning, what would be the worst-case scenario(s)? For example, is it a ransomware attack that could result in the leak of sensitive information? What about one that locks up production systems? Mass pwning of firewalls and edge devices? What about a business email compromise (BEC) that results in a $100,000 bank transfer to attackers? Would falling for the North Korean fake worker scheme cause big problems?

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Vaughn stressed that once identified, these should be ranked by pain to the business. She added, five to eight "painful" items are a reasonable number to determine.

Vaughn ranks risk in three categories: existential, painful, and annoying. Existential risk means that a breach would close the doors of the business. Painful risk equates to business disruption with associated costs and bad press. Annoying risk is something that can be fixed semi-easily.

A key piece of determining your risk profile is understanding who sees you as a target. Do state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups have your organization in their sights? Or is your business most likely to be targeted by BEC scams? Are ransomware affiliates trying to find a way into your systems? Do you have a large inventory of software or appliances that are high on attackers' hit lists? How is your patching hygiene, and do you have bugs that are known to be exploited?

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

This type of intel is free and available from sources like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), but can also come from private threat intelligence services. Vaughn recommended that CISOs and security leaders lean on their vertical Information and Analysis Centers (ISACs) as well.

"That’s your most valuable resource," Vaughn said. "And it's free."

Items that fall between both the "worst-case scenario" and "who's targeting you" lists are where teams need to start first. "Every overlap is a scenario," Vaughn explained. "Write one sentence for each: who, how, against what, and costing what?"

In terms of a BEC attack, Vaughn pointed out a simple phone call verification could be the most effective prevention, and it costs nothing. "Find where the attack stops for the least money," Vaughn advised. "Spend in that order."

Additional free controls that actually work, according to Vaughn, are multifactor authentication (MFA) everywhere, which is something she adds is "non-negotiable" and urges CISOs to "fight for." An asset inventory is also invaluable, even if it's just a spreadsheet, and of course it "beats doing nothing." Patching bugs that have already been exploited, resisting the urge to give everyone admin credentials, and testing backups also make the list. And for ransomware, having backups isn't enough; network segmentation has to go along with it.

"If you can't restore from backups, or you don't have backups, you have hope," Vaughn said. "Hope is not a control."

She pointed out that nothing on this list of controls can be bought from a vendor. "There's no SKU for 'turn on MFA' and 'keep a spreadsheet,'" she added.

It might be tempting for cybersecurity teams to try and tackle these four questions on their own, but Vaughn said that including management in these conversations will help better align priorities to the broader business and will help management understand the potential fallout of not taking care of cybersecurity.

There are some best practices for doing this; for instance, Vaughn recommends linking spend to a business outcome: "If nobody funds a CVE, we stop shipping for a week," is one example she offered.

She also recommends bringing three spend options, with prices attached, and then making a recommendation for one. Additionally, Vaughn said CISOs and cyber teams should never promise "security," only reduced risk, and discuss investment decisions from that lens.

Offer, say, options that cost "$12K, $4K, or zero," she explained. "Zero means we accept the risk, so I recommend the $4K."

And once the decision is made, Vaughn suggested an email follow-up like, "Confirming we’re deferring X and accepting the risk of Y. Tell me if I got that wrong." That paper trail can prove invaluable following a compromise, she said.

InfoQ Homepage News Amazon ECS Gateway Arrives with Generated Hostnames and No Custom Domain Support

Nov 04, 2026 3 min read

AWS recently released Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level ingress resource that lets platform teams define networking once, and application teams attach services to it with a connector. Each service gets a generated hostname, and neither the announcement nor the documentation describes how to put a custom domain in front of it.

The gateway is described by principal developer advocate Channy Yun as:

a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

It is available in all commercial regions where ECS runs, at no additional charge beyond the resources it provisions. The first question practitioners asked was how to put their own domain in front of it.

The split it introduces is organizational: platform teams create a gateway with its infrastructure IAM role, subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and optional WAF web ACLs, then associate it with clusters. Application teams add a gateway connector through CreateService or UpdateService, and for each service ECS provisions an ACM certificate, a hostname, a listener rule, a target group, and a security group that accepts traffic only from the load balancer.

Amazon ECS Gateway architecture. (Source: AWS News Blog post)

On Reddit, commenter zurnout went straight at the hostname:

I don’t get how this is useful at all since you get a random domain name for your ecs service. How am I going to direct traffic to that? It’s the same thing with ECS Express.

Asked whether a CNAME would solve it, he explained why it would not:

It creates host-based rules in the load balancer, so it wouldn’t know where to route if you used a CNAME.

Commenter ResponsibleWaltz1479 reached the same conclusion, calling the feature usable "for ephemeral /preview environments if the app is not hostname aware," but not for their existing setup.

The documentation supports the reading: each service "gets a generated hostname in the form https://.ecs..on.aws," and "Amazon ECS uses host-based routing to direct requests from a shared Application Load Balancer to the appropriate service." Custom domain names, Route 53, and CNAME records go unmentioned. Commenter Kralizek82 raised the one workaround nobody resolved, asking whether a gateway could serve as an internal CloudFront origin.

Opinion split on whether the service is substantial. Commenter bioJesusMain called it:

It could even just be a CDK construct on top of ALB/NLB and Route 53

Commenter brokenlabrum answered that from experience:

Those higher level L3 constructs have often turned out to be a mistake because they need to expose every knob on the L2 constructs they wrap. And if they’re opinionated and don’t, ejecting from an L3 construct without it deleting your resources is hell.

Commenter Aggressive-Height167 put the case for it, noting that letting a cloud team define networking once while application teams deploy against it "seems like a pretty solid improvement." The test, they added, "is whether it actually removes complexity without taking away too much control."

The documentation adds a cost detail the announcement leaves out. A gateway adds load balancers as existing ones fill and removes them only when they empty, but it "does not consolidate load balancers" and "does not move services between load balancers, so several partly filled load balancers can remain after services leave." Each one is billed.

Commenter jregovic noted that more than 25 services means more than one load balancer. An AWS respondent answered that "multiple ALBs are handled by the gateway itself - so it’s not something that you need to worry about." The gateway does handle them, but it does not pack them, so the count still climbs with the number of services.

ECS also "does not repair changes made outside it," so modifying or deleting a managed resource means traffic "can stop," and later deployments, gateway updates, and cleanup operations may fail.

The limits are specific: twenty-five services share one load balancer, against a default maxAlbCount of 10 and a documented ceiling of 200 per gateway, and AWS warns that "if maxAlbCount is reached and no ALB has available capacity, the deployment fails." Listeners serve HTTPS on port 443 only, services must use awsvpc networking in the same VPC and account, and Express Mode services are excluded altogether.

The thread’s most upvoted comment dismissed the launch as "a promotion project," and several commenters asked why AWS Elastic Beanstalk did not already cover the ground, one pointing at its Cluster Mode release last month. On the other side, dmcnaughton1 said a current ECS migration was early enough to adopt it.

#9952. Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

An unreleased version of the AI model has found and chained multiple vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux, Anthropic says.

An unreleased version of Claude identified critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used browsers and operating systems and chained them into working exploits requiring little or no human interaction, Anthropic said this week.

The exploits included one that enabled data theft from a locked Android smartphone, another zero-click exploit allowed remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on Linux servers, and a third that could have allowed attackers to remotely crash Windows systems. In total, Anthropic said, the model generated five working exploits targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. All affected vendors have addressed the vulnerabilities after Anthropic reported them.

The exploits are the latest evidence that frontier AI models are moving beyond simply identifying individual flaws to combining multiple into sophisticated working exploits. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said in a blog post this week.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Historically, creating such chained exploits would have required special teams with domain expertise, the researchers wrote. "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Anthropic's report described a one-click RCE exploit chain involving Chrome on macOS. The exploit combined four vulnerabilities in Chrome's JavaScript engine, memory protections, browser process isolation, and federated sign-in functionality.

Each of the vulnerabilities that Claude discovered helped overcome a different security control and allowed the chained exploit to escape the browser's sandbox. As a proof of concept, Anthropic's exploit launched macOS Calculator from Chrome when a user loaded a malicious webpage.

Anthropic said it reported 62 vulnerabilities to Google, all of which had been assigned CVE identifiers, rated high or critical, and patched by Chrome 156.

"For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers," Anthropic said. The exploit chain combined four weaknesses Claude identified in Safari — a use-after-free flaw in Safari's JavaScriptCore engine, a way to bypass WebKit's Gigacage memory protection, a vulnerability in the WebContent sandbox, and a JavaScriptCore flaw.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Apple has since fixed the issue, Anthropic said.

The Android exploit, meanwhile, targeted a locked Google Pixel 9. Claude chained three vulnerabilities in Android's device-transfer and USB-handling mechanisms, bypassing four layers of protection to extract photos and other personal information from the phone without unlocking it. Anthropic said Google has addressed the issue.

Claude's Windows exploit, which Microsoft has patched, involved a remotely exploitable denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. The flaw was an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's implementation of the transport protocol used by HTTP/3. An attacker could send a small number of specially crafted network packets to a vulnerable server to crash it and repeatedly trigger crashes, disrupting access for users, Anthropic said.

For Linux, Claude developed a zero-click exploit against the kernel's networking stack that would have let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute commands with root-level privileges on affected servers, without requiring any user interaction. "This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches," Anthropic said.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

With AI getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, defenders need powerful models for patching them before attackers can exploit the flaws, Anthropic said. "Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do," the company said.

To that end, the company is expanding access to its most capable AI models for vetted cybersecurity professionals through its Cyber Verification Program. The program now has three access tiers that give security teams a way to apply for the level of access appropriate for their work.

"It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward," Anthropic said. "Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever."

Andrew Bolster, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, says Anthropic's results are credible where they can be verified. The Chrome, WebKit, Windows, and Linux fixes are all public, he notes, but any claims that Claude discovered them autonomously are Anthropic's own. "The report gives no success rates, cost, or human-hours per chain, which is critical context for security leaders," he says.

Some of the conditions for the exploits to work were also noteworthy, he says. For instance, the Android chain involved a stolen phone and a USB cable, and the Linux exploit required an exposed MPTCP listener. "Exploit benchmarks show model success dropping sharply once ASLR, stack canaries, and sandboxing are enabled, and VulnCheck found only 1.3% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities confirmed exploited in the wild," Bolster says. "Delivery, reliability, and target preconditions remain the attacker’s problem for now, though I'd expect that gap to narrow."

Claude's chained exploits are another indication that AI has lowered the barrier to discovering vulnerabilities and building working attacks, says Jacob Krell, senior director, secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs. But there are still substantial barriers between a proof of concept and a reliable attack in the wild. "A shell on one honeypot tells you little about the next server's worker count, build, or kernel," Krell notes. "AI has made finding the bug cheap. Getting it to work on a server it has never seen is still the expensive part."

At the same time, the gap between a proof of concept and a reliable, broadly deployable attack is increasingly becoming about time and target-specific adaptation rather than specialized expertise, he cautions.

Defenders are making a mistake if they assume this kind of vulnerability discovery always requires the most powerful AI models, adds John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security. "Local systems, including a Mac Studio with 128GB of memory or a DGX Spark, can support AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research. The target, model, tools, and operator's skill matter."

It may take attackers longer, with less capable systems, and attacks may be more practical only against smaller, less-scrutinized code bases. But defenders need to account for that capability, Strand says. "If AI can find vulnerabilities in Windows, Android, Linux, and Chrome, what does that say about code that receives a fraction of that attention? Think about your IP cameras. Think about the firmware on the router running a remote office. All of that is in play."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.
